text:
I started exploring AI when I was still at school.
Not with Python. Not with GPUs. With a soldering iron 🔧.

Around 1990, a 𝗭𝗫 𝗦𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗺 — an 8-bit home computer — appeared in our home.
And that was it. Love. 🖤 One that, honestly, continues to this day.

Back then, it wasn’t just a computer — it was a 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗸𝗶𝘁.
You had to 𝘴𝘰𝘭𝘥𝘦𝘳 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘬𝘦𝘺𝘣𝘰𝘢𝘳𝘥. For real. Every single key.
Assemble the boards. Put everything into a case.

The case was awful, by the way. 😅
 So I built my own — wooden.
 And moved the keyboard out separately.
 Console + keyboard. I had my own vision 🙂

After that, I started programming. Small things. Experiments.
 I wrote a couple of programs.
 I don’t even remember what the first one was about.
 But there was an 𝗮𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺 — and I made it work.
 That was enough for me back then.


___________


Around 2000, when I was 16, things got really interesting.
That’s when I started reading a paper magazine called 𝘊𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘶𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘳𝘢.
It explained early AI research papers in plain language, for a broader audience.

Btw, those ideas later led to the 2024 𝗡𝗼𝗯𝗲𝗹 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗣𝗵𝘆𝘀𝗶𝗰𝘀,
awarded to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton 
for foundational work behind neural networks and machine learning. 🏆

What fascinated me wasn’t AI as a buzzword,
but the 𝘴𝘪𝘮𝘱𝘭𝘪𝘤𝘪𝘵𝘺 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘣𝘦𝘢𝘶𝘵𝘺 of how it actually works.

Why is AI slow and expensive?
Because every time it predicts the next word, it goes back to check if it makes sense.
By the fourth word, you’re already dealing with millions of checks.
Exponential complexity. Classic. ⚡

Those papers suggested a simple idea:
𝗱𝗼𝗻’𝘁 𝗯𝗿𝘂𝘁𝗲-𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 — 𝗰𝘂𝘁 𝗼𝗳𝗳 𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗲𝗻𝗱𝘀 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆.

I applied this to formal mathematical logic.
Instead of hours or days to prove the Pythagorean theorem,
I got it down to about 𝟯𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘀 —
on an 80286 computer with a 16-bit processor. 🖱️

Just by teaching the algorithm to notice earlier:
 — this makes no sense
 — we’ve already been here
 — this leads to a loop 🔄

That was my first AI-related program.
It made me a member of the Junior Academy of Sciences of Ukraine.
I was in 11th grade.

And this curiosity hasn’t gone away.

Even today, AI interests me not as a shiny button,
but as a system —
𝘸𝘩𝘢𝘵’𝘴 𝘪𝘯𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦 𝘪𝘵, 𝘸𝘩𝘺 𝘪𝘵 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘬𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘢𝘺 𝘪𝘵 𝘥𝘰𝘦𝘴, 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘸𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘳𝘦𝘢𝘭 𝘭𝘪𝘮𝘪𝘵𝘴 𝘢𝘳𝘦.

𝗗𝗶𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝘆 — 𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗹𝗶𝗳𝗲?🤔
